SECTION: I. (Pages 3-6)

TOPICS: ballot-access requirements, third-party and independent candidates, constitutional challenges, First Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, equal protection, nomination petitions, qualifying fees, procedural history, appellate review

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The Libertarian Party, along with voters and prospective candidates, sued the Georgia Secretary of State over ballot-access requirements for third-party and independent candidates seeking office in the U.S. House of Representatives (Page 3)
- The court reverses in part, affirms in part, and vacates the district court's injunction (Page 3)
- The court concludes the district court erred in finding Georgia's ballot-access requirements violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments (Page 3)
- The court agrees with the district court's determination that there was no equal protection violation (Page 3)
- To appear on the ballot for a non-statewide office, third-party and independent candidates must submit a nomination petition signed by 5% of the total number of registered voters eligible to vote in the last election for the office (Page 3)
- This case is before the court for the second time, referencing Cowen v. Georgia Sec'y of State, 960 F.3d 1339 (11th Cir. 2020) (Page 3)
- Candidates have a 180-day period to collect signatures for nomination petitions (Page 4)
- Each signer must declare they are a registered voter qualified to vote, sign their name, and include their residential address; dates of birth are encouraged for verification (Page 4)
- Upon filing, a notarized affidavit must be attached stating signers were qualified, and an official must verify the signatures (Page 4)
- A denied nomination petition can be reviewed by a court via a writ of mandamus (Page 4)
- Prospective candidates for non-statewide office must file a notice of candidacy and submit a qualifying fee (Page 4)
- The fee is 3% of the office's annual salary for most offices, including U.S. Representative (Page 4)
- A candidate who cannot afford the fee may file a pauper's affidavit, requiring an oath of inability to pay, a financial statement, and a signed petition (Page 4)
- Under Georgia law, a "political party" is defined as a political organization that nominated a candidate receiving at least 20% of the total vote cast in the preceding general election (Page 4)
- Ballot-access requirements differ for third-party candidates running for statewide vs. non-statewide office (Page 5)
- Candidates for statewide office can avoid the petition requirement if nominated by a third-party "political body" that meets specific criteria (Page 5)
- A political body can nominate statewide candidates if it files a qualifying petition signed by 1% of registered voters or nominated a candidate who received 1% of the vote in the preceding general election (Page 5)
- Otherwise, a candidate for statewide office can earn a place on the ballot by submitting a nomination petition signed by 1% of registered voters eligible to vote in the last election for the office (Page 5)
- The Libertarian Party challenges this system with two constitutional claims: an unconstitutional burden on associational and voting rights, and an unjustified classification (Page 5)
- The case involves the Libertarian Party and the Secretary, with claims related to First and Fourteenth Amendment rights (Page 6)
- The district court initially granted summary judgment to the Secretary on both claims (Page 6)
- On remand, the district court ruled for the Libertarian Party on its First and Fourteenth Amendment claim (Page 6)
- The district court permanently enjoined the enforcement of the 5% signature requirement for non-statewide office candidates (Page 6)
- The district court imposed a 1% signature requirement as an interim measure until the state legislature enacts a permanent replacement (Page 6)
- The Secretary and the Libertarian Party both appealed the district court's ruling (Page 6)
- The court reviews the district court's decision on cross-motions for summary judgment de novo, citing Chavez v. Mercantil (Page 6)
